summary: 4 worth fixing. Everything else looks fine.

findings.title: Camera video can be watched without a password
findings.found: IPC-Living-Room (192.168.1.120) sends its live video to anyone who asks, without a password.
findings.means: Anyone connected to your Wi-Fi can open the video feed. No device has asked your router to open it to the internet (we checked); unless you set up a port forward for this camera yourself, people outside your home can't reach it.
findings.likely: Moderate: it needs someone on your Wi-Fi, like a guest, a neighbour who knows the password, or an infected device.
fix: Open the camera's app or web page.
Go to Settings → Network or Security and turn on "Authentication" for RTSP (sometimes called "RTSP password" or "Stream encryption").
If you don't use the camera with other apps, turn RTSP off completely.
Run Porchlight again to confirm.

findings.title: Android debugging is open to the network
findings.found: Living Room TV (192.168.1.140) accepts connections on the Android debugging port (ADB, port 5555). This is common on Android TV boxes and some phones.
findings.means: On many devices this lets anyone on your network install apps and control the device without a password. Some ask for permission on screen first; many TV boxes don't.
findings.likely: Moderate: it needs someone or something on your network, and malware that spreads between Android TV boxes looks for exactly this port.
fix: On the device, open Settings → Developer options (or System → Advanced → Developer options).
Turn off "USB debugging", "Network debugging" or "ADB debugging".
If you can't find Developer options, the maker may have left it on by default: check for a firmware update.
Run Porchlight again to confirm it's closed.

findings.title: WPS is on for "HomeNet-EXT"
findings.found: "HomeNet-EXT" (broadcast by your PIX-LINK extender at 192.168.1.115) announces WPS, the "press a button or type an 8-digit PIN to connect" feature. WPS is already off on "HomeNet".
findings.means: The PIN part of WPS has a known design weakness: on some devices, someone within Wi-Fi range can work out the PIN with free tools and get the Wi-Fi password, however long it is. The push-button part is fine.
findings.likely: Low to moderate: it needs someone within range of your Wi-Fi, and it only works on some models. Turning WPS off costs nothing unless you connect devices with the WPS button.
fix: Open your PIX-LINK extender's settings page (http://192.168.1.115/) and log in.
Find WPS (usually under Wireless, Wi-Fi or WLAN) and turn it off, then save.
Run Porchlight again to confirm it's off.

findings.title: A network with no password is using your Wi-Fi's name
findings.found: Another access point nearby broadcasts "HomeNet" with no password. It doesn't belong to your router or extender.
findings.means: Phones and laptops join networks by name. A copy with weaker protection can trick a device into joining it, and whoever runs it could then see that device's unencrypted traffic.
findings.likely: Low to moderate: it could also be a neighbour whose router happens to use the same name. It matters more if your Wi-Fi name is unusual.
fix: Don't connect to it. On your phone, a copy usually shows without a lock icon.
If any of your devices saved that open network, tell them to forget it.
Give your Wi-Fi a name that's unique (not your family name or address), so copies stand out.
Run Porchlight again later to see if it's still there.

findings.title: Make sure the Wi-Fi extender has its own admin password
findings.found: PIX-LINK (192.168.1.115) has a settings page at http://192.168.1.115/.
findings.means: Anyone on your network can open that page. Porchlight never tries passwords, so it can't tell whether the factory password (often blank or "admin") is still set. Whoever knows it can change the device's settings.
findings.likely: Low, once you've set your own password.
fix: Open http://192.168.1.115/ in a browser.
If it lets you in with no password or with "admin", set your own (12+ characters) in its System, Management or Admin settings.

findings.title: A new device joined your network
findings.found: New since your last checkup (13 November): Living Room TV (192.168.1.140).
findings.means: Usually that's a new phone, a guest, or something that was switched off last time. If you don't recognise it, someone else may know your Wi-Fi password.
fix: Check the device list below: its type and address can help you recognise it.
If you don't recognise it, change your Wi-Fi password in your router's settings, then reconnect your own devices.

findings.title: Devices can't open doors to the internet on their own
findings.found: Your router answered our UPnP check but doesn't offer automatic port opening (UPnP-IGD is off).
findings.means: Programs and devices on your network can't open a way in from the internet without you setting it up. That's the safer setting.

findings.title: Your 2 Wi-Fi networks are well protected
findings.found: "HomeNet" uses WPA2. "HomeNet-EXT" (broadcast by your PIX-LINK extender at 192.168.1.115) uses WPA2.
findings.means: That's the current standard. Its real strength is the password: 12+ characters that aren't a name or a date is what keeps it safe.
findings.likely: Nothing to do. If your router offers WPA3, you can switch later.

findings.title: This computer's firewall is on
findings.found: Windows Firewall is on for the network you're using (private profile).
findings.means: Other devices on your network can only reach the programs on this computer that you've allowed.

findings.title: Fixed since your last checkup
findings.found: Old file-sharing service (FTP) is on (Your router (Home Router)).
findings.means: Porchlight checked again and these are gone. Nice work.
